en: Then, for the successful accomplishment of sacrifice, one should resort to a region such as Brahmāvarta,
which is inhabited by Brahmanas and abounds in sacrificial fuel, flowers, and excellent water.
It was devoted to the Dharma, free from calamities for the various social classes, abundant in earth,
kusha grass, medicinal herbs, and cattle, devoid of atheism, and irreproachable.
The conjunction of autumn and spring is most excellent for the performance of the rite of initiation;
in their absence, the rainy season is recommended, and otherwise, any other time as well.
In initiation and consecration, as well as in the formal reception of mantras, in the undertaking and release of vows, and in rites involving the handling of ritual substances; || 4 ||
On the full moon day of Kārttika and Vaiśākha, during an eclipse of the sun,
at the solstices, the equinoxes, and when Jupiter is in its transit, one should perform sacrifice.
On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śrīśaila, and the Himavat mountain;
on Pāriyātra, Arbuda, Vindhya, Śuktimat, and the Rakṣa mountain.
In the Gaṅgā, in the Yamunā, and in the space between them;
in the Sarasvatī, the Dṛṣadvatī, the Godāvarī, and in the ocean.
At the confluence of the Narmadā with the Kṛṣṇavarṇā, likewise at Pañcanada, near the Tuṅgabhadrā, and from the vicinity of the Candrabhāgā. || 8 ||
In the sacred bathing places of secret shrines, at the confluences of rivers, in delightful mansions, and in forests and groves; 9.
There, one should examine the ground, ensuring it is free from depressions and elevations, not saline, not damp, and devoid of mud and sand. (10)
Free from husks, hair, and stones, devoid of ashes and charcoal, liberated from wicked thorns, smooth, substantial, and firm. || 11 ||
The ground, free from the shapes of winnowing baskets and the like, sloping toward the northeast,
purified by the tips of his fingers, and tested by digging with his nails— [he prepared it].
A ground that is complete with leaves, colors, and other qualities, which bestows the fruits of one's desires,
which brings delight to the mind, and which leads to liberation or spiritual perfection as described.
It was dug by Bhūpadeva with a supreme weapon and filled [with earth];
it was purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and treated with decoctions of medicinal herbs.
Having obtained such a vast earth, which resembles the surface of a mirror and is well-enclosed on all sides, one should perform the supreme maṇḍala sacrifice. || 15 ||
The full moon day, the eighth day of the bright fortnight, and likewise the fourteenth day—these lunar days are for rites of prosperity;
those of the dark fortnight are for rites of liberation.
The days beginning with Citrā and those other lunar days (tithis) that are traditionally prescribed—
these too, because they are conducive to the constituent parts of the sacrifice, should be accepted in the performance of the sacrificial rite.
The three Uttaras, Revatī, Rohiṇī, the constellation presided over by Bṛhaspati, Anurādhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and Ārdrā are purifying, as is the constellation presided over by the Pitṛs. || 18 ||
The Nairṛta, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, and likewise that presided over by Pūṣan—these fourteen are praised in the sacrifices to Śiva. || 19 ||
One should abandon eleven [days] because they are indicated by their names alone;
he who is composed should begin the sacrifice on the remaining days.
And one should smear the purified sacrificial ground, covered with a canopy,
with cow-dung taken from a bull that has not yet stepped upon it.
Equipped with all ritual offerings, bathed, wearing white garments, and pure; wearing a turban, adorned with rings, and having his body consecrated with the protective marks (kala); || 22 ||
With his body anointed with sandalwood paste and adorned with garlands and ornaments, the mantra-practitioner shall dispel the obstacles situated upon the sacrificial ground. 23.
Having sprinkled them with auspicious water and then with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should subsequently sprinkle them with fragrant water consecrated by the recitation of the Aghora weapon mantra.
Having descended to the ground with flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and sesame seeds, one should worship Śiva;
thereafter, the wise man should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the collection of Śiva-mantras.
Once the formal acceptance has been made and the earth and fire have been thus consecrated,
one should cause the construction to be carried out on the second or the third day from that of the deity.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Instruction on the Directions such as that of the Preceptor, in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṅgraha.
